name: Ageing of paint on Victorian iron
describes: Linseed-oil paint oxidises, hardens and slowly chalks; its gloss falls to a satin and then a matt bloom. Iron is repainted every few decades, so each campaign adds a scheme and the film thickens: detail softens, arrises round, hollows fill. Under a glass roof the paint also gathers the court's soot and dust on every upward face, heaviest high up where warm air carries it. The film fails first where it is thinnest or where water lies: at arrises, bolt heads, rivet heads, joints and the shoes, and there rust breaks through and runs.

insideGrime.text: Inside, a Victorian court's grime: soot of gas and of London's air settles under the glass (walls darken toward the springing), dust on every ledge.

drivers.driver: water standing at joints, shoes and bolt heads

photograph: A thick, soft-edged paint film, satin to matt with age, dusty on its tops; chips at arrises showing older colours; small rust blooms at bolt heads and joints.
